claims.text: The Odeonsplatz was developed in the early 19th century by architect Leo von Klenze and marks the southern end of the monumental Ludwigstraße.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Before 1827, the square was known as Fürstenplatz or Reitschulplatz, named after an old riding school that was located there.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The square was renamed Odeonsplatz in 1827 after the Odeon, a concert hall commissioned by King Ludwig I and built by Klenze on the west side of the square.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The Odeon building and the identical Palais Leuchtenberg were both modelled on the Palazzo Farnese in Rome.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Today, the former Odeon concert hall houses the Bavarian Ministry of the Interior, while the Palais Leuchtenberg serves as the Bavarian State Ministry of Finance.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: An equestrian statue of King Ludwig I, designed by Ludwig von Schwanthaler, was added to the square in 1862.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The square has traditionally served as a major venue for parades and public events, and the annual parade to the Oktoberfest still passes through it today.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: On November 9, 1923, the square was the site of a fatal gun battle that ended the Beer Hall Putsch, resulting in the deaths of four state police officers and sixteen Nazis.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: During the Third Reich, a memorial for the fallen Nazis was erected near the Feldherrnhalle, and all passersby were required to perform the Hitler salute; the memorial was demolished in 1945.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Adolf Hitler was captured in a famous 1914 photograph taken at the Odeonsplatz, showing the crowd celebrating the outbreak of the First World War.
claims.subject: self
